thread.title: Don't Confuse Price and Value When it Comes to AAPL

author: Martin Tillier
title: Don't Confuse Price and Value When it Comes to AAPL
text:
Apple (iStock photo)
For the last two years, the stock market has been consistently underestimating Apple ( AAPL ). Around that time, I started to point that out to investors, and have done so on many occasions since. Now, with the stock outperforming the broader market and hitting new highs, I am sure many people are looking at the stock as expensive and are thinking of taking a profit.
I am usually all in favor of that, but to do so in this case would be a mistake. Apple, even at these levels, still represents one of the best values around.
That may be hard to believe when you look at the chart a few paragraphs below, but when it comes to stocks, value is not about how you feel about price, it is a measurable thing. The three main measures of value are trailing price to earnings ratio (P/E), forward P/E and the ratio of P/E to expected growth (PEG).
The forward-looking measures forward P/E and PEG inevitably involve predictions of future performance, so by nature contain some speculation and risk.
Trading and investing, however, are all about predictions and risk, so forward P/E and PEG are more useful than looking at what happened last year or last quarter.
Expectations of growth vary by sector and industry, so the best way to use those metrics is to look at them in relation to other, similar businesses. In Apple’s case that means comparing the forward P/E and PEG with the members of the group that has become known as the FAANG stocks, Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Netflix ( NFLX ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ). Those four and Apple all operate in different industries, but as mature companies with tech backgrounds they make for a reasonable comparison.
The forward P/E for the FANG stocks are, in order of the acronym, 21, 27, 71.62, and 22.92. AAPL, meanwhile, may look high on the chart but is trading at a forward multiple of 14.31.
When growth is factored into the calculation, AAPL has a PEG ratio of 1.15, as compared to 0.87 for FB, 4.71 for AMZN, a whopping 71.67 for NFLX, and 1.42 for GOOGL.
On that basis, one could say that FB is better value, and GOOGL is at least close, but when the tow metrics are taken together it is clear that AAPL is undervalued.
The most interesting question to me is why that is the case, and why the pessimism has persisted through two years of being proven to be wrong-headed. Much of it is to do with what I mentioned earlier, the perception that because the price of AAPL is high it cannot represent value.
Oscar Wilde once said of young people that they knew “...the price of everything, but the value of nothing,” and that looks to be true of traders and investors when it comes to Apple.
There are also other, more valid concerns. Despite their tech background, Apple’s main business is as a manufacturer, and there are fears that the market for their main product, the iPhone, is saturated. That argument, however, rests on the assumption that people will at some point cease upgrading, which comes under the category of “I’ll believe that when I see it.”
The saturation argument has been around for years, but the continuing desire for the latest phone and growth in huge markets like China and India has rebutted it every time.
The thing is, Apple’s detractors have been saying the same things for years and have been wrong every time up to now. I guess at some point they will be right, if only on the “broken clock” principle, but until that time comes I will trust the data and evidence, which clearly suggest that Apple is still a tremendous value stock to buy.
